item.title: Trump’s Top Trade Representative Details Offer That Canada Rejected
item.description:
The United States had offered to reduce its tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos, and eliminate a recently imposed tariff on Canadian lumber, before negotiations suddenly collapsed last night, Jamieson Greer, the U.S. trade representative, said Saturday.

In an interview with The New York Times, Mr. Greer detailed previously confidential and unreported elements of the U.S. trade offer to Canada, saying those measures would have given Canada the most preferential treatment of any trading partner.

Trade talks between the countries suddenly soured late Friday night, following a week of talks in which negotiators appeared hopeful for an agreement.

Mr. Trump had abruptly threatened Canada with a 50 percent tariff on about $20 billion of its exports in July, in an effort to push the country into making trade concessions and removing certain practices the United States had deemed unfair.

Those tariffs were set to go into effect on the morning of Aug. 19. But on the night before, Mr. Trump delayed the tariffs until Aug. 22, saying that the countries had a deal, “subject to the finalization of documents.”

But over the following days, and particularly late into the night Friday, that consensus crumbled. It fell apart over a series of issues that, individually, may have seemed small but collectively represented a big division over issues of importance to both sides.

Mr. Greer said that the Trump administration had pledged to eliminate the 10 percent tariff on softwood lumber that Mr. Trump imposed last year using a provision known as Section 232.

The United States had also offered to reduce a 25 percent tariff on cars that Mr. Trump put in place last year. But because Canada qualifies for a further reduction when the cars contain any amount of U.S. content, the automotive tariffs could have gone as low as 7 percent, he said.

The United States also offered to lower tariffs on metals, one of Canada’s most important priorities.

“The United States was prepared to reduce the tariff on steel from 50 percent to 25 percent for the majority of steel Canada sent to the United States,” Mr. Greer said. Steel would be subject to what is known as a tariff-rate quota system, in which only a certain amount of steel imports would receive that lower tariff.

On aluminum, the United States had offered to reduce its tariffs to 25 percent from 50 percent without such a quota limitation, Mr. Greer said.

For products made with steel and aluminum, like golf clubs and beer cans, the United States offered to cut those tariffs by anywhere from 10 to 25 percentage points, with the lowest tariffs set at 15 percent.

Mr. Greer said that the United States had also offered to suspend the 50 percent tariffs that it brought into effect early Saturday morning on Canadian dairy, wine, hockey sticks and others goods.

“Obviously, we would completely suspend the 50 percent Section 338 tariffs that we were going to apply to 5 percent of Canadian exports,” he said, referring to the tariffs that went into effect Saturday.

The Canadian government did not immediately respond to a request to comment on Mr. Greer’s description of what Canada had left on the table when it suspended talks Friday evening.

In a televised briefing earlier Saturday, Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, slammed the U.S. proposal as a “bad deal.” He added, “we cannot accept what they offered and we will not give what they asked.”

Mr. Carney said that Canada had walked away from negotiations not just because it assessed that what was being offered by the United States negotiating team was insufficient, but also because U.S. officials were asking for concessions that Canada was not prepared to make.

He said Canada had equally agreed to meet many American demands, including pulling all its retaliatory tariffs on U.S. steel, aluminum and cars, as well as convince its provinces to restore the sale of U.S. liquor, which most of them have banned.

But, he said, the United States refused to include certain tariff exemptions for heavier trucks. Mr. Carney said the United States also asked for concessions that would affect Canada’s culture and maintenance of protections for the French language and demanded that Canada take out tariffs against non-U.S. trading partners, without offering sufficient benefits for Canada to do so.

Canada had demanded better tariff treatment for pickup and semi trucks in the final stages of the talks, as well as more tariff exceptions for cars made with U.S. and Canadian content, three people familiar with the negotiations said.

“In short, they asked too much and offered too little,” Mr. Carney said about the United States in his Saturday address.

In the interview, Mr. Greer argued with that assessment.

“These are modifications that would continue their best access and improve it,” he said.

Matina Stevis-Gridneff contribute reporting from Toronto.

item.title: Someone Was Impersonating Her in Online Affairs. She Says It Was Her Husband.
item.description:
As evening approached on a Thursday in late March, Collien Monica Fernandes, a German actress and television personality, was growing restless. She was having an especially hectic day, shooting an episode of a TV series in a busy marketplace in Phu Quoc, Vietnam. The extras needed wrangling; the set was adjusted and readjusted. As the hours wore on, she checked her phone compulsively — she wanted to be alone in her room by 6 p.m. Finally, at 5:45, with the tropical light dimming, the director called it a wrap. Fernandes tore off her costume, raced to her nearby beachside hotel suite and made sure the digital “Do Not Disturb” sign was on. No one who worked on the show had any idea of what she was about to do.

Fernandes had recently finalized her divorce from another celebrity, an actor and comedian named Christian Ulmen. Ulmen was famous for being a master of cringe humor, or as the Germans call it with more precision, fremdscham (“someone else’s embarrassment”) humor — the kind that comes from watching another person experience an excruciatingly humiliating situation. In his most successful show, “Jerks,” Ulmen played a hapless actor and comedian also named Christian, whose desperate efforts to avoid awkward scenarios only dig him into deeper holes of shame. Escorts, sexual insecurities and fecal preoccupations feature prominently in the show, as do elaborate lies that pile up and eventually collapse beneath the men who lean on them.

Over the course of their 14-year marriage, Fernandes and Ulmen were a high-profile couple in Germany and the media covered their relationship regularly, often presenting it as a modern egalitarian marriage that reflected strong feminist values. After they had a child in 2012, Fernandes started speaking in interviews about the double standards applied to working mothers; she published a series of children’s books challenging traditional gender roles and produced a three-part documentary about the history of feminism. Ulmen, meanwhile, made news by declaring that he was taking a year off after their daughter was born.

At times, the public attention felt uncomfortable or outright invasive. When Fernandes gave birth to their daughter, she said, tabloids knew even before she had left the hospital room. Ulmen was obsessive about preserving their privacy — a journalist who was a friend of Ulmen’s wrote in a magazine profile that Ulmen seriously considered moving when the package delivery man started asking too many friendly questions. More troublingly, Fernandes was subjected to disturbing online harassment that went far beyond the usual comments about a female celebrity’s appearance. For years someone, or multiple people, had been impersonating her on social media, starting online affairs with men and creating and sharing or just recirculating pornography purportedly of her — material that featured other women who resembled her or imagery that might have been A.I.-generated. Others were charging money for the promise of access to her.

Fernandes initially did not devote much energy to the problem — how would she ever find these trolls typing away in some remote corner of the globe? — but in 2021, she learned about a video in which she appeared to be having sex with numerous men. She decided to respond as a journalist, by investigating her digital harassers. She was plagued by these shadowy figures for years and after considerable effort, she believed she had finally found one of them, a man who was conducting sexually explicit online affairs in her name. That March evening, she was ready to expose him.

The action Fernandes was about to take would dominate the news in Germany for weeks, inciting a nationwide movement that many would compare to #MeToo in the United States. Alone in her hotel suite, she prepared a post on Instagram to go up around the same time as the publication of a major news report about her experiences. She announced to her quarter of a million followers that she had filed a criminal complaint in Spain, where she had been living for the past few years, against a man she believed was responsible for digital and psychological abuse. “The perpetrator was (as I now know) quite close the whole time,” she wrote. “His name: Christian Ulmen.”

Fernandes first learned in 2020 that she was being impersonated. Men began reaching out to her team, each with a similar, bizarre request: They wanted to confirm that it was, in fact, the real Collien Fernandes who was flirting with them on social media, who sent them nude photos and videos of herself, who was engaging in phone sex with them. Fernandes started to sense the magnitude of the problem when a lunch with a producer took a strange turn — he was clearly under the impression they were in some kind of online affair. “Suddenly he was showing me photos of me in bikinis — erotic photos,” she says. Fernandes made it clear she would never have sent him those kinds of photos and she had no idea who had.

By then, Fernandes had been married for nearly a decade. She and Ulman met in 2010, when he was 34 — already a well-established director and actor — and she was 28, a presenter on a popular music video channel in Germany. That spring, Fernandes had posed seductively on the cover of the men’s fashion magazine FHM Germany, which named her the sexiest woman in the world. Soon afterward, Ulmen cast her as his wife on a show he was making called “The Snobs,” which was set over 18 holes on a golf course, with Ulmen playing an insufferable, self-made businessman.

Fame had made Fernandes skittish about dating, especially as she felt people underestimated her because of her public image. The tabloids often characterized her as a “party girl,” because she was frequently photographed at celebrity events; but Fernandes considered herself something of a nerd. She was driven, even a workaholic, an obsessive researcher with a critical eye. The network she worked for, she recalls, wanted her to be bubbly, ask inane questions and keep things light, which wasn’t really her sensibility: She had an irreverent edge, and would sometimes go off script on live shows, which could get her into trouble with producers, even if the audience seemed to appreciate it.

Fernandes and Ulmen hit it off on the set of “The Snobs.” On their first date, Fernandes recalls, they talked for nine straight hours. They both started out on camera early, as teenagers, and they found in each other something of a haven. “We could have really deep conversations,” Fernandes told me. Neither had much interest in Germany’s celebrity-circuit nightlife; they preferred to stay home, talking late into the night about the people in their lives, their gripes with the industry or what made a scene funny. “It looks like German television now has a new dream couple,” an entertainment magazine wrote after they went public with their relationship.

Fernandes successfully transitioned out of her younger starlet image, becoming a pundit and journalist, while still acting; Ulmen’s work was widely lauded in the press, even if it sometimes courted controversy. He occasionally appeared in sketches, interviewed celebrities or gave interviews in character as his comic alter ego, a boorish, offensive figure named Uwe Wöllner who was prone to crude sexism. As Wöllner, he hosted a hidden-camera show called “Who Wants to [Expletive] My Girlfriend,” in which women in relationships competed to see which of them could most easily lure other men into going on a date or even having sex (promised but never delivered). Ulmen characterized the work as feminist satire that skewered male sexual desperation, but he sometimes joked about identifying with Wöllner’s adolescent impulses. “I, too, have wondered if it isn’t actually the case that I’m really Uwe Wöllner,” he told a magazine in 2013, “and only pretend to be Christian Ulmen the rest of the time.”

Fernandes also sometimes felt confused by the two versions of Ulmen — the one who presented himself to the public as a feminist and the one she says she saw in her own home. After announcing that he was taking a year of parental leave, Ulmen resumed working. In later years, Ulmen sometimes parented solo while she was on location, but she says he was often resentful and jealous. Seemingly small irritations were enough to provoke his anger, such as the placement of a package in the hallway or her mentioning something in the press that he considered private, like the kind of cookie they preferred. (Ulmen’s lawyer did not respond to multiple requests for comment.)

In the criminal complaint she filed in Spain in December 2025, Fernandes portrayed their domestic life as volatile; she said she never knew when Ulmen might lose control. She alleged physical abuse. In 2023, people near their home in Mallorca heard a woman screaming for help from a window and someone called the police. The officers brought both Fernandes and Ulmen to the station, and Ulmen was held overnight on suspicion of domestic violence. No proceedings were pursued by the authorities, and Ulmen’s lawyer has denied that there was any one-sided violence or threats during that incident.

In legal proceedings over press coverage, Ulmen’s lawyer tried to challenge the reporting of physical violence and threats against Fernandes. Ulmen denied Fernandes’s allegations in an affidavit, according to the lawyer. As in all criminal proceedings, the accused is presumed innocent until proved guilty — a principle that has been emphasized in the German media coverage on the case.

At the time, Fernandes told her sister about alleged abuse (which her sister confirms), but she shared none of it with her friends. She had become deeply private, especially after small details of her life were leaked to the media by people she thought she could trust. She also worried that her friends might not understand why she still had hope for the marriage. “I thought I could fix it,” she told me. “I just needed to find the right therapist to help us come out of those negative patterns.” Her husband was imperfect and impulsive, with some serious anger problems, she always thought. But he was also her best friend.

Because Ulmen often seemed suspicious of her interactions with other men, Fernandes hesitated before telling him about her unsettling lunch with the producer who believed they were having an affair. She told me she was surprised that Ulmen asked no follow-up questions — he didn’t even want to see the exchanges — which, in retrospect, she thinks might have been telling.

A chance booking as a commentator on a news talk show ultimately led Fernandes to the active pursuit of her digital abusers. On the set, Fernandes met a lawyer named Josephine Ballon, a founder of HateAid, a nonprofit dedicated to helping victims of online harassment. Their conversation about Ballon’s work hit home: Fernandes was still disturbed whenever she thought about the explicit video that featured someone who looked like her having sex with many men. She decided to make a documentary about sexual digital abuse. The title was “Deepfake Porn,” a topic the project addressed while also exploring other aspects of online sexual exploitation of women.

Fernandes decided to weave her own story into the documentary, even though she sensed her husband disapproved of that approach. She wanted to try to track down some of the people who were impersonating her online; she especially hoped to unveil the person who seemed to be starting digital affairs on her behalf with people in her social circles.

In researching the documentary, she interviewed a man who had been contacted by one of her impersonators on social media. He explained that the fake Collien had initiated phone sex with him on a Google Hangout, but the voice didn’t sound like Fernandes’s. The impostor Collien had also sent him a pornographic story in which a terrified Fernandes is raped by numerous men. It ends with her collapsed on the floor, covered in semen.

Taking in that story and viewing various images of herself as part of her research, she had an overwhelming sensation of shame. She knew these were not pictures of her, or things she had done, and yet they seemed to represent her. They evoked a torturous trick the mind plays when it’s presented with something horrifyingly self-incriminating that is known to be fake but looks deceptively real.

Fernandes resolved to set a trap for the impersonator. She knew that one of her impersonators was operating through a fake Collien Fernandes account on LinkedIn. She and her producer used the producer’s husband’s LinkedIn account to message the impostor account. The plan was to discuss something innocent — an upcoming birthday party for Fernandes — to see if the impersonator would start talking about sex. They anticipated that the conversation might reveal clues about the person’s identity. Fernandes told me she was so enthusiastic and hopeful about the idea that she mentioned it to Ulmen — but the person behind the account never responded.

In the end, the documentary Fernandes made was unable to identify her impersonators, though it detailed some of her efforts to find them. The film aired in December 2024, not long before Ulmen and Fernandes flew from their home in Mallorca back to Germany to celebrate Christmas with their families. They planned to spend Christmas Day with Ulmen’s family, but Ulmen asked if they could stay at the hotel instead. Fernandes described to me what she says happened next in their hotel room: Ulmen had said he had a stomachache; in fact, he had just read a news item about the documentary, which mentioned that Fernandes went to the German police to file a criminal complaint against her anonymous impersonators, something Ulmen was unaware of. Ulmen asked question after question, growing more and more agitated until he was visibly shaking. Finally, he told her to sit down, because he had to tell her something. Secrets he’d been guarding for close to a decade came out, haltingly, she says: He had been impersonating her online.

That night, Fernandes recalls, Ulmen was in a panic. She suspects he feared that the police would arrest him and that he might spend years in prison. According to Fernandes’s criminal complaint in Spain, Ulmen told her that he had messaged hundreds of men over the course of 10 years, but he would not tell her which men, only that she knew some of them. Fernandes, stunned, made recordings of parts of their conversations, which were included in the complaint. She had so many questions: What did he think would happen if he got caught? Why, of all people, had he impersonated her to start a sexual online affair with their pension insurance salesman? Ulmen tried to answer. He was curious to know who liked her. The whole thing felt like something separate from their true relationship, he tried to explain, more like using porn with some elements of reality. (Asked to comment on Fernandes’s allegations through his attorney, Ulmen did not respond.)

For Fernandes, the digital abuse she believes Ulmen committed was more of a betrayal than even his alleged physical attacks. She could explain away spontaneous violence as a result of anger someone struggles to curb in the moment. But she felt this humiliation was premeditated. It was the difference between someone committing murder in a blind rage, Fernandes says, and someone who plans to “murder women and put them in the fridge and give them to the dog.” She believed her husband had not just used her for his and others’ sexual gratification — he had also erased her as a person, replacing her with a depraved adolescent’s version.

Fernandes later obtained and included in her complaint logs of conversations that she alleges came from Ulmen’s laptop that she captured in video footage on her phone. They were, according to the allegations in the complaint, conversations that Ulmen had with ChatGPT over the days that followed, in which the user inquires, for example, about how to ask men to delete emails, without committing some kind of witness tampering.

Fernandes, meanwhile, fell into a paralyzing depression. She couldn’t fathom how she could return to working and socializing with the men in her life, any of whom might think she was crazy, that she had hit on them, that she had sent them pornography — naked photos with her legs spread, violent rape fantasies. She wasn’t entirely ready to end her marriage, much less publicly accuse Ulmen — and yet if she didn’t reveal that she believed her husband was the impersonator, how could she continue promoting a documentary that demanded justice for herself and all other victims of digital abuse?

Fernandes had not made a decision by the time her family flew back to Mallorca after the holiday. In an email that Ulmen sent to his lawyer, which The New York Times has reviewed, he confessed to his lawyer to conducting sexually explicit digital affairs impersonating Fernandes with about 30 men. He also expressed regret. Fernandes told me that Ulmen heard back from a lawyer a few days later, while they were out grocery shopping. She waited by the car in the parking lot while her husband wandered away to hear his lawyer’s counsel.

A lawyer advising a client in that situation would most likely reassure him that in Germany, disputes between couples, short of those involving physical violence, are considered low priority by prosecutors; they often encourage couples to work out their problems in divorce court or civil court (where damages are much lower than would be true for comparable offenses in the United States). An impersonator who posted degrading images publicly would face a stronger legal challenge than one who circulated them to individuals, as Fernandes was alleging; but either way, in Germany, first-time offenders of nonviolent crimes almost never see prison time. In practice, German law focuses on rehabilitation rather than retribution, says James Q. Whitman, a professor of comparative law and foreign law at Yale Law School.

The more Fernandes learned about how little German law was likely to do to deliver some sense of justice, the more outraged she became — not just about her own specific experience, but about the failings of the law to help so many women who had little recourse when strangers sexually violated them online.

Fernandes had been numb since her conversation with Ulmen on Christmas. But when Ulmen returned from talking to his lawyer, she flew into a rage in the parking lot. “So you’re telling me that it’s possible to digitally abuse me and nothing happens — and you think that’s OK?” Fernandes recalls yelling at him. “Do you realize the situation? That you’re talking to the victim?” She says Ulmen told her to get in the car — that she was acting insane. People were going to recognize them. Fernandes was embarrassing him.

Over the next several months, Fernandes wrestled with whether or not she was ready to leave her marriage. “I’m lying in bed,” she told me, recalling the period following his confession. “I can’t work anymore. I feel bad. I don’t have any motivation. I’m suffering.” Her husband, meanwhile, appeared relatively content, she says.

In June, Fernandes told Ulmen to move out. With time, it became clear to her what she wanted to do, which was bring a criminal case against him — but to bring it in Spain, where the couple had lived for the past two years. and where there was a more comprehensive legal infrastructure to address digital harassment, including a court specifically dedicated to addressing violence against women (which many U.S. states have, but which Germany does not).

The news of an explosive criminal complaint was unlikely to stay under wraps for long. After Max Hoppenstedt Heinrichs, a journalist at Der Spiegel, learned of the complaint, he and a fellow investigative reporter, Juliane Löffler, did extensive research and interviewed Fernandes at length. The article they published on March 19 was titled “You Digitally Raped Me” — a quote from a text Fernandes sent Ulmen when she was still trying to convey to him the gravity of what he had done. The article reported that Ulmen allegedly physically abused his wife, impersonated her online and circulated sexual photos of women who could easily be mistaken for her.

The incendiary Instagram message that Fernandes posted from her hotel room in March was timed to the publication of Der Spiegel’s article. In the post, she decided not to mention the physical violence that she says was part of her marriage, focusing instead on the alleged digital abuse. Germany already had laws on the books to prevent domestic battering, but lagged behind many other countries in how it regulated sexual exploitation and violence online. She wanted to focus attention on the lack of those specific protections She hoped that in calling attention to those gaps in legislation, she might help change the law as well as the culture.

Collien Fernandes’s allegations elicited the kind of widespread rage in Germany that was unleashed in the United States when the Harvey Weinstein story broke. Protests erupted across the country, including one in Hamburg with more than 20,000 people. “The shame has to change sides,” some signs said, referencing a phrase popularized by Gisèle Pelicot, the activist whose shocking public testimony against her husband and dozens of men who raped her while she was drugged had stirred a similar awakening in France. Other signs said, “It’s always a man!” and “Everyone knows a victim, no one knows a perpetrator.” A magazine columnist wrote that her inbox was full of messages from women saying, “How are we supposed to live with men?” and that they planned to stay celibate. Leading politicians rallied around the cause of offering women better protection from digital violence.

The response from fellow German celebrities on social media was swift. Benjamin von Stuckrad-Barre, a widely respected journalist and TV personality who had been a friend of Ulmen’s for close to 30 years, wrote on Instagram that his “solidarity and support” belonged solely to Fernandes. An actress named Inez Bjorg David, who appeared on “Jerks,” posted a copy of the email she had just written to her managers. “I would love it if you removed ‘Jerks’ from my résumé,” she wrote. “It makes me want to throw up and I’m so angry.”

The day the news broke, Stephanie Hubig, the German minister of justice, went public with proposed legislation, long in the works, intended to protect the victims of digital abuse. The legislation would criminalize making or distributing A.I.-modified sexually explicit images without consent, an offense subject to two years’ imprisonment. She also called for technology platforms to disclose information about secretive social media accounts so that violators’ identities could quickly be revealed. Even deepfakes or impersonations that were not sexual in nature but caused reputational harm could be subject to prosecution under the legislation.

Fernandes was gratified that those in Parliament were paying attention, but the timing of the announcement about the legislation contributed to a powerful backlash. Commentators sympathetic to the AfD, Germany’s far-right, populist party, along with anti-establishment actors, privacy rights activists and other critics cast Fernandes, in thousands of posts on X, as colluding with Hubig to try to chip away, for example, at the right to be anonymous online.

Other commentators implied, on social media or in the press, that the madness of the crowd was undermining the presumption of innocence, that women were generalizing too broadly about all men as bad actors (“Throw Out Toxic-Femininity” was the headline of one story about Fernandes in a German magazine). Critics accused Fernandes of having posed practically nude anyway, of being a man-hater, an attention seeker, a bad mother.

It’s not uncommon for individuals who step forward with stories of sexual harassment or domestic violence to face a backlash in Germany, says Löffler, one of the reporters for Der Spiegel who broke the Fernandes story and who has published prominent #MeToo journalism. Until recent years, detailed reporting on accusations of domestic abuse or sexual harassment in Germany were rare, and when it did appear, it often provoked critiques from readers and commentators. “You might get feedback like, ‘Why do I need to hear about this private affair?’” she says. Only in recent years, Löffler explains, has there been more recognition that writing about these issues is an important way to expose abuses of power.

It is not only a cultural norm that has often muffled this sort of reporting in Germany. The German Constitution considers inviolate the right to dignity. That principle is understood there to include privacy and the right of “personality,” which is thought to be, at its core, the right to control one’s own image. Although the German Constitution also ensures the right to free speech, courts in Germany are forever balancing the two concerns, which has had a notable effect on the way that the German media operates. In the United States, a public figure who is trying to win damages against a media outlet must prove that it published false information and also showed “actual malice” in doing so. In Germany, public figures can bring charges of “insult” even if the facts reported are accurate, and courts are frequently asked to weigh in on whether a given piece of journalism is sufficiently important to the public interest to justify exposing the personal details it includes.

Certain details — such as those about sexual leanings or revelations unveiled in therapy — may be deemed so private that no measure of public interest would justify their publication. Courts in Germany are also swifter to file injunctions halting publication than their U.S. counterparts. (The right to privacy in Germany extends so far that mug shots and even the last names of those accused of crimes — including sexual harassment and terrorism — are routinely excluded from news reports, unless there’s a strong public interest.)

The emphasis on privacy has often resulted in a somewhat muted media response to cases in which public figures are accused of sexual misconduct. By contrast, in the United States, the initial #MeToo reporting about Weinstein unleashed unfettered coverage in numerous publications about other harassers or abusers in positions of power, as women stepped forward to share their own stories.

Shortly after Der Spiegel published its story, Ulmen’s lawyer quickly announced that he would be taking legal action against the magazine, accusing it of publishing illegal reporting and making false claims, while also warning away other publications from reporting on Fernandes’s allegations. Ulmen’s lawyer would go on to contest the allegations of physical assault, insist that his client never created or disseminated deepfake videos and challenge the inclusion of the email Ulmen sent to his lawyer.

Even though Der Spiegel never stated in the article that Ulmen had created or distributed deepfake videos of Fernandes, an appellate court ruled in June that the article implied that Ulmen had done so because the story explored the phenomenon of deepfakes. The publication was required to add new language to the article that explicitly stated that there was no evidence that Ulmen made or distributed deepfake videos. Der Spiegel was also ordered to delete two sentences deemed highly personal from Ulmen’s correspondence with his lawyer.

Although Der Spiegel had strong evidence to support its reporting, including audio files, documents, text chats and photos, some news outlets were reluctant to reference Der Spiegel’s reporting on Fernandes’s allegations. In Germany, publishers often fear relying on other publications’ reporting unless they, too, have strong evidence in hand. (In the United States, by contrast, once information about public figures is public, other outlets can reference it, unless they know it’s false.) Much of the coverage defaulted to stories about the legal maneuverings on each side.

Ulmen’s lawyer, in winning small victories in court, was able to sow doubt, in some corners, in Fernandes’ credibility or the accuracy of her story. Reporterfabrik, a nonprofit devoted to media literacy, is scheduled to release a report in late September on how the media narrative about Fernandes played out; in an Instagram post announcing the report, the nonprofit wrote that Ulmen’s lawyer has operated by “disputing trivialities and using the tactic of hyperspecific denials — to desperately create the impression that [Ulmen’s] ex-wife accused him unjustly.” They call the approach “a grotesque web of distractions, half-truths and sham battles, intended to disappear behind a smoke screen of flashbangs.”

The right to control one’s image in Germany has also translated into journalistic norms that are not enforced by law but nonetheless give unusual power to sources. People can often expect to have approval over their quotes before they are published. In March, Ulmen spent five hours talking about his marriage to reporters at Die Zeit, a weekly newspaper. In the end, Ulmen opted to rescind the entirety of the interview. “Mr. Ulmen Would Rather Not After All,” the headline of the story said. (Ulmen’s lawyer later said that the interview was always intended to be a “background briefing.)

That Der Spiegel was as challenged as it was in reporting on Ulmen, can seem paradoxical: Out of legal deference for Ulmen’s right to control his image, the publication was limited in what it could say about his alleged digital usurping of his wife’s image.

Although many of Ulmen’s fans defended him on social media, the allegations and the article in Der Spiegel had immediate professional consequences for him. The German streaming service that carried “Jerks” pulled the show from its site. Producers also chose to shelve a new project, a show called “The Au Pair,” that Ulmen had been working on in the months after his split with Fernandes.

Fernandes was surprised, when journalists who had obtained the scripts ran them by her, to see intimate details that she says he had taken from their family’s personal life and woven into the story lines. In one episode, according to journalists who reported on the scripts, a young man admits to his love interest that he has posted pictures of her on sexualized sites, because it aroused him to see other men’s desire for her. The scene ends with him weeping.

“Shame is a pain that hurts less when you share it,” Ulmen once said in an interview, explaining why the men on “Jerks” so often ended up exposing, inadvertently or not, their most base impulses. In another interview, he is described as never feeling more free than when he plays Wöllner, a figure who does not bother laboring under the burden of hiding his shame. In a 2013 article called “My Friend, the Monster,” a journalist friend of Ulmen’s at the time wrote: “There’s one role that really gets to him: being Christian Ulmen. How does that even work? Nobody tells you.”

I spoke to Fernandes several times over the course of the summer. She was still regularly appearing on TV to push for more significant penalties for digital offenses committed against women, while also trying to manage the anguish that the news inevitably created for members of her family. The criminal complaint she filed in Spain with a special court devoted to violence against women was awaiting a ruling on jurisdiction from a higher court; the original complaint she filed in Germany during her research for the documentary in 2024 had been closed, then reopened following the prominence of the news story, then transferred to a different court, and is still in an investigatory phase. A news release from that court reported that prosecutors were still assessing the material they had with regard to both bodily injury and “allegations of ‘digital violence.’”

When we talked, she often looked to be in a state of shock, something that was rarely visible in the dozens of interviews she gave for German media, in which she invariably projected confidence and poise. She often wore a black blazer, an item of clothing she seems to rely on for added authority, even though it’s so oversized that she appears to be retreating into it. Because she’s more petite than people assume, barely 5-foot-4, she used to be able to move freely without being recognized. More recently, she said, she is approached constantly. “I get hugged a lot in elevators,” she said. “The older women — they want to tell me they went through something once, too.”

The last time we met, in June, we sat on her porch in Mallorca. The Mediterranean seemed to hover in the distance, calm and blue. Fernandes told me that she has a hard time relaxing these days; she has struggled with anxiety, panic attacks and insomnia. Ulmen still lived nearby, and she dreaded running into him at the gas station or the mall or even, possibly, at her own front door. She was overwhelmed by the avalanche of attention, some of it negative. At times she even seemed to feel she had to justify why she decided to speak out. She said she had learned nothing from her husband about which men in her social circles had been contacted by her impersonator. “I had to be able to speak up for myself,” she said.

Despite the backlash, much of the legislation the German justice minister has proposed has wide support and could pass next year. Fernandes is now thinking about returning to Germany. Moving to Mallorca had the effect of largely isolating Fernandes, who, even now, speaks only enough Spanish to get by at the grocery store. She has few close friends who live nearby, and the multimillion-dollar homes closest to her are all protected behind high gates.

Her own house feels oddly empty, with two different rough patches on walls where flat-screen televisions used to be before Ulmen took them to his new home. Holes were still visible where there used to be security cameras. Ulmen had arranged for them to be installed soon after they moved in. One of the cameras in Fernandes’s office faced into the room, rather than out toward where intruders might be approaching. Months after Ulmen moved out, the video feed was still available to him, she worried; she didn’t have the passcode to shut it off. Last winter, a friend who was visiting took one look at the cameras and decided they had to go. “Do you have a ladder?” she asked Fernandes.

The cameras came down.

item.title: A Murder Trial in Massachusetts
item.description:
In the hours before the courthouse in Plymouth, Mass., opens, hundreds of women clad in pink have been massing outside. They’ve come to support Lindsay Clancy, the mother on trial for killing her three young children, ages 5, 3 and 8 months.

In almost any other case, it would be an odd declaration of allegiance. But Clancy is not a typical murder suspect. She attempted for months after the birth of her third child to get treatment for what she reported was her increasing postpartum derangement. Then she killed her children, she has admitted, in what she says was a state of psychosis. Closing arguments begin tomorrow. (Here’s what to know about the trial.)

Should she be treated like an ordinary killer? That question is a Rorschach test for Americans fascinated by this case. Some say Clancy was failed by a system that doesn’t take postpartum mental illness seriously enough. “It should not take tragedy for people to pay attention to mental health,” said Renee Kimball, the organizer of the courthouse demonstration.

Other people are horrified by arguments like that, saying they ignore the facts of this incomprehensible crime. “I don’t look at her and feel sorry for her,” said the former Fox News host Megyn Kelly. “Three kids are dead!”

Whatever the jury decides, for many people the case has become a proxy for all manner of perceived societal ills.

One perspective on this calamity remains straightforward: Clancy killed her children and must pay the price. That is the view of the prosecution (which has charged her with first-degree murder, a crime with a mandatory life sentence) as well as several pundits. A headline on one conservative site put it this way: “Lindsay Clancy Defenders Are Just as Sick as She Is.”

But others see her case as evidence of a nation that neglects new mothers and fails to properly care for maternal mental health. Clancy, a labor and delivery nurse who experienced debilitating insomnia and other symptoms, visited the emergency room twice, went to a day program, called a suicide hotline and checked into a residential program, which discharged her. “I really need help,” she messaged her psychiatric nurse practitioner. She reported intrusive thoughts, received therapy over Zoom and got 30 prescriptions for 13 medications. But nobody ever diagnosed her with postpartum psychosis, an emergency that would have warranted hospitalization.

For that reason, many view the children’s deaths as a product not of individual depravity but of a broken medical system. Hundreds of women have posted on social media about their own postpartum struggles and expressed empathy for Clancy. Allie Beth Stuckey, a conservative Christian commentator and a fan of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., told her viewers that she had a split reaction when she heard about the case. She felt “immediate disgust and anger,” she said, but also a recognition of “how dark and how out-of-control for some women postpartum can be.”

Our thinking about cases like these has changed over the decades.

Twenty-five years ago, a Texas nurse named Andrea Yates drowned her five children in the bathtub and then wrapped them in sheets. Her defense, too, said she was suffering from psychosis. (She wanted to be executed, though, because she believed that the Devil lived within her, her lawyer, George Parnham, said in an interview.) The jury found her guilty, but she got a new trial and was found not guilty by reason of insanity.

After that, Parnham pushed state lawmakers to adjust the strict definition of insanity and to allow a lighter sentence for mothers with postpartum mental disorders. He made little headway then, but now people are more open about mental illness. “We don’t think about people who struggle mentally as automatically just not tough enough, malingerers — just fakers — in the way that we might have 20, 30 years ago,” said Michelle Oberman, a legal scholar who has studied cases of mothers who kill.

Today, some three dozen countries offer juries an option between murder and insanity, one that recognizes the particular mental vulnerabilities that can arise after birth and set a significantly lower penalty for mothers who kill an infant. One similar bill has passed in the United States, in Illinois.

Still, the question of whether mental illness diminishes culpability remains in dispute, and many states in recent decades have made it harder to use an insanity defense. (The tide began to turn when a jury acquitted John Hinckley Jr. on the basis of insanity after his attempted assassination of President Ronald Reagan.) Five states have eliminated the insanity defense altogether.

In cases like the Clancy killings, the debate may boil down to this: Is the crime so heinous that insanity cannot excuse it, or is it so heinous that only insanity can explain it?

item.title: Carney Stands Up to Trump in Trade War Despite the Risks
item.description:
On Friday night, Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada did something that few other world leaders before him have dared to do.

After days of intense trade negotiations with the United States, with less than an hour to go on a midnight deadline for a new round of tariffs from the Trump administration, Mr. Carney instructed his negotiators to walk away.

Then, he announced that once 50 percent tariffs came into effect on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, he would order retaliatory tariffs on the United States “dollar for dollar.”

In a statement, Mr. Carney said he had gone into the trade talks in good faith, seeking “the best deal for Canadians” but “never a deal at any price or on any deadline.”

By walking away, Mr. Carney chose a road that no major U.S. ally has taken: With his country’s economy on the line, he stood up to President Trump and refused to accept the administration’s offer of a new trade relationship with tariffs permanently baked in. Britain, the European Union and other major U.S. trading partners have agreed to smaller deals that have been volatile and often left them worse off.

The collapse of the talks came after Mr. Trump declared on Tuesday that the deal was practically done.

Mr. Carney never echoed that. Over the week, as negotiators spent long hours in Washington huddled in the office of the U.S. trade representative, Mr. Carney appeared optimistic but insisted that there was still work to be done.

Until there wasn’t.

Each side now claims that the other introduced new or unreasonable demands at the last minute — the kind of finger-pointing that is common when trade talks fall apart.

Make no mistake, Mr. Carney has a lot to lose.

Canada, which is closely integrated with the United States and relies on it for defense, is heavily dependent on trade with its superpower neighbor. In his statement, Mr. Carney acknowledged the cost of his choice for many Canadians by saying that his government would work to support industries and companies affected by the new tariffs.

It will also be costly for U.S. residents, who have been paying for Mr. Trump’s tariff policies through higher prices that have also been driven by the war in Iran and spiraling oil costs.

But on Friday, Mr. Carney appeared resolved to shoulder the costs of his decision. And he has risked Mr. Trump’s ire before.

In a speech in Davos, Switzerland, in January, he described a new era in which the United States was no longer a guarantor of stability and where middle powers like Canada have to unite to survive. The speech — and its enthusiastic global reception — angered Mr. Trump.

Mr. Trump has also been riled by Mr. Carney’s outreach to China, which led to a narrow but significant trade agreement this year; by Canada’s persistence on banning the sale of U.S. liquor; and by the Carney government’s retaliatory measures against the United States for its broad, devastating tariffs on core Canadian industries.

Since he rose to lead Canada last year, Mr. Carney has put in motion a plan to help his country survive Mr. Trump’s presidency and, in the long run, thrive apart from the United States. One of his favorite lines is that “nostalgia is not a policy,” and he has told everyone who will listen that there is no going back to the old relationship with the United States — a close and familial, if lopsided, bond.

Instead, Mr. Carney has been traveling to secure new partnerships in Asia and Europe, a generational shift away from economic dependence on the United States, although that is unlikely to bear fruit fast enough to cushion the blow of the breakdown of the two countries’ relationship.

It’s likely that Mr. Trump will not take kindly to Mr. Carney’s trade decision. Just before beginning his second term, Mr. Trump said he was willing to inflict “economic pain” on Canada to get what he wanted. He has repeatedly expressed a desire to make Canada the 51st state, describing it as little more than a vassal that “lives because of the United States.”

But Mr. Carney’s vision for Canada, with a surprising assist from Mr. Trump’s needling, has ignited a wave of patriotism. Going into the trade talks, more than half of Canadians — many more than those who voted for Mr. Carney — said they wanted him to give nothing away.

Several premiers of different political stripes expressed their support for Mr. Carney after his decision. Doug Ford, a conservative who leads Ontario, cheered him on. David Eby, the progressive premier of British Columbia, said, “We didn’t ask for this, but we’ll keep fighting for as long as it takes.”

Not everyone is enthusiastic. Danielle Smith, the conservative premier of Alberta, who has good relations with the MAGA movement, was more circumspect and urged Mr. Carney to return to the negotiating table. Canada’s industry is aghast with the prolonged turbulence and uncertainty that Mr. Trump’s trade war against Canada, and Mr. Carney’s refusal to submit, are causing.

But there is little doubt that Mr. Carney will also be cheered, at home and abroad, for doing what he thought was best for his country, and for saying, in his Friday statement, that “we will not allow any nation to determine our future.”

item.title: Mexican Governor Accused by U.S. of Aiding Cartel Leaves Office, Again
item.description:
The governor of the Mexican state of Sinaloa — who returned to office on Friday despite accusations by U.S. prosecutors that he had conspired with a cartel — reversed course on Saturday after widespread criticism, particularly from members of his own party.

The governor, Rubén Rocha Moya, said in a social media post on Saturday night, about a day and a half after returning to office, that he had requested an indefinite leave of absence.

In April, U.S. prosecutors unsealed an indictment accusing Mr. Rocha and nine other current and former Mexican officials, including a sitting senator, of taking part in a broad conspiracy to help the powerful Sinaloa cartel traffic drugs into the United States. A few days later, he stepped down — the first time.

The indictment set off a scandal in Mexico and drove a new wedge between the U.S. and Mexican governments.

Mr. Rocha has denied wrongdoing and called himself the victim of a political attack. But his return drew opposition within his own party, Morena, including from Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum. Hours before Mr. Rocha’s announcement on Saturday, Ms. Sheinbaum, a leader of Morena, wrote on social media that public servants should not place personal ambition above the well-being of the people. She criticized what she called “the naked ambition of power for power’s sake.”

“Mexico deserves public servants who understand that positions are temporary,” she wrote, “but responsibility to the nation is eternal.” Although she did not mention Mr. Rocha by name, it was widely interpreted in Mexico as a criticism of his return to office.

Others in Mr. Rocha’s party were more pointed. Governors and senators from Morena released statements saying that he had acted alone and stressing the importance of respecting an active investigation. Ricardo Monreal, an influential Morena politician who had supported Mr. Rocha, called on him to go back on leave.

In the U.S. indictment, prosecutors accused Mr. Rocha of accepting bribes and help in getting elected in exchange for protecting the cartel, which has terrorized his state and Mexico for years. Ms. Sheinbaum has repeatedly said that her government is not protecting the governor, but has also called for more evidence from U.S. officials and supported Mexican’s investigation into the accusations. Mexican officials said in April that the United States had not provided sufficient evidence to support its request for Mr. Rocha’s extradition.

Mr. Rocha, 77, is the highest-ranking member of Morena, Mexico’s dominant left-wing political party, to be indicted by the United States. The case against him is the Trump administration’s most significant public step in cracking down on the corruption that it says is at the heart of Mexico’s cartel problem.

When he took leave after the indictment, Mr. Rocha said he wanted to participate in the Mexican government’s investigation as an “ordinary citizen,” without the immunity afforded to his office Experts said on Friday that returning to office restored his constitutional immunity.

With his departure one day later, he has presumably lost it again.

item.title: Canada-U.S. Trade War: What to Know
item.description:
Talks between the United States and Canada failed late Friday to head off steep new tariffs on Canadian goods, prompting Canada to promise “dollar for dollar” retaliation.

Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada said he had suspended the talks because the American side had introduced last-minute terms that were “unfair, uneconomic and called into question the reliability of any deal.” Then on Saturday, in a powerful speech to Canadians, Mr. Carney said Canada was under attack by President Trump’s tariffs and was “at war” with the United States.

He did, twice. On Tuesday, he said the two countries had reached a deal aside from some details and had extended an earlier deadline that would have introduced the new tariffs.

On Friday, only hours before the two sides announced the collapse of the negotiations, Mr. Trump said he thought a deal could be reached.

Mr. Carney blamed last-minute demands for the collapse of negotiations. He said, among other things, that American negotiators pushed to roll back Canada’s efforts to promote Canadian, including French-language, content in online streaming services; subsidies for industries like publishing and film production; and even mandatory labeling in French as well as English on packaging. French is an official language in Canada.

Speaking to reporters on Friday, a U.S. official said Canada wanted concessions that the United States wasn’t prepared to give, particularly when it came to the automotive sector, as well as trade in steel, aluminum and lumber.

Slamming the U.S. proposal as “a bad deal,” Mr. Carney’s forceful speech on Saturday made it clear that he considered Mr. Trump’s tariffs an attack on Canada. “We’ve recognized from the start that America has changed,” he said. “We recognize that sometimes, its signature is written in pencil.”

“We cannot accept what they offered and we will not give what they asked,” he added. “We were not prepared to compromise Canada’s sovereignty or undermine our key industries.”

Mr. Carney, who is burnishing his reputation as a leader who will stand up to Mr. Trump, said Canada would retaliate against the new tariffs “to protect our workers and businesses.”

The United States had offered to reduce its tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos, and to eliminate a recently imposed tariff on Canadian lumber, before the negotiations suddenly collapsed, the U.S. trade representative, Jamieson Greer, told The New York Times in an interview on Saturday.

Early Sunday morning, Mr. Trump wrote on his social media platform, Truth Social, that Canada wanted the “benefits of being a State, without being one!!! They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!”

But he did not seem to respond directly to Mr. Carney’s muscular speech against the United States.

The new tariffs account for $20 billion of the $382 billion worth of products Americans bought from Canada last year and cover a wide array of goods, from fake mustaches to dog leashes.

The full list of more than 500 products can be found here, here and here.

The lists single out several industries, particularly forestry, a sector long targeted by the United States. Building products, especially plywood, are affected, as well as other products like tissue used to make toilet paper. Dairy products, clothing and alcohol are also on the lists.

Many of the tariffs are on products like honey that often come from small businesses, likely without the financial means to withstand a substantial loss of business for any sustained period.

The collapse of the talks also means that Canada did not roll back the tariffs of up to 50 percent that Mr. Trump put on the auto, aluminum and steel industries last year. The president also added 10 percent tariffs on softwood lumber tariffs of 35 percent.

The tariffs came into effect on Saturday. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs come into effect on Sept. 8, Mr. Carney said.

The government has yet to unveil its list. But Mr. Carney said it would largely target “steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, electronics.”

Doug Ford, the premier of Ontario, Canada’s most populous province, is urging Mr. Carney to place export taxes on oil, gas and electricity, as well as critical minerals. Energy is, by far, the largest Canadian export to the United States.

Yes. Since Mr. Trump began his second term, relations between the United States and Canada have been strained.

Not only has Mr. Trump targeted Canada with tariffs, he has insulted its leaders, suggested the border is an arbitrary line, and repeatedly proposed the nation be annexed as the 51st state. He said he was willing to inflict “economic pain” on Canada to get what he wanted, and recently said the country only “lives because of the United States.”

In a speech in Davos, Switzerland, in January, Mr. Carney said that the United States was no longer a guarantor of stability, and that middle powers like Canada must unite to survive. The speech, and its enthusiastic global reception, angered Mr. Trump.

Also, on July 1, Canada’s national holiday, the Trump administration declined to renew the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement on trade for another 16 years. That means the agreement will now undergo annual reviews.

Asked how the new U.S. tariffs will affect the agreement’s continued renewal, Mr. Carney said, in French, that “it certainly isn’t good news.”

item.title: The World’s Breadbaskets Are Getting Pounded by War, Weather and Trade Spats
item.description:
Instant noodles. Hot chapatis. Sliced bread.

Wheat is at the heart of the modern diet, and this year, it is facing an accumulation of modern dangers. The breadbaskets of the world are getting pummeled by drone strikes and devilish weather, nudging prices higher amid already soaring food costs in the wake of the Iran war.

Heat and drought have diminished harvests in some of the biggest wheat-producing countries, including the United States, which is expected to have its worst wheat harvest in a half-century, spiking prices. Poor countries that agreed to buy American wheat under the threat of Trump tariffs could be stuck paying abnormally high prices.

The Black Sea, a crucial passage for the global wheat trade, is an active theater of the Russia-Ukraine war, while the Houthi militia’s attacks on shipping in the Red Sea have already forced grain shipments to take a longer, more expensive route around South Africa.

Beyond that, a supercharged El Niño further threatens water levels in the Panama Canal, while drought has reduced water levels to perilously low levels in transit routes like the Rhine and Danube rivers in Europe, raising transportation costs. All this at a time when the global atmosphere is hotter than normal because of a century of fossil fuel burning, threatening the livelihoods of small farmers in poor countries.

The simultaneous troubles reveal the risks inherent in the global food system today. Only a few crops, like wheat, provide most of the world’s calories. Relatively few governments dominate the export of wheat, including Russia, Canada, the United States, Ukraine, and the European Union. Their customers are mainly low-income countries that no longer grow much of the food their people eat.

“The system we currently have in place depends on three things: seamless trade, cheap energy, stable climate,” said Evan Fraser, a professor who studies the global food system at the University of Guelph, in Ontario. “Today, it seems none of these assumptions are met.”

Few things are as politically potent as the price of bread, and wheat prices were already at a three-year high in July, according to the Food and Agriculture Organization. The U.N. agency has warned of higher prices later this year.

The saving grace is that the world had a bumper crop of wheat last year, and global stocks remain strong. The risk, said Monika Tothova, an economist who specializes in commodities at the Food and Agriculture Organization, is that “several sources of uncertainty begin to reinforce one another.”

“A combination of El Niño-related weather impacts across major exporters, renewed constraints on Black Sea exports and further disruptions to key shipping routes would have implications far beyond wheat production itself,” she said.

Russia and Ukraine together account for nearly a third of the wheat that the world buys. This year, just as harvests began, their grain shipments have nearly ground to a halt.

In recent weeks, both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up their attacks on each other’s grain export terminals and ships in the Black Sea, a waterway they share to get their goods out to the world.

In the critical Russian Black Sea port city of Novorossiysk, grain terminals suspended operations after a drone attack in early August.

That attack followed a Russian bombing campaign against the Ukrainian port city of Odesa, which Ukraine relies on to get its grain out. A potential alternative, the Danube River, is far more difficult to begin with — and this year, the Danube’s water levels have plummeted because of drought. When Russia invaded Ukraine and blocked its Black Sea grain trade in 2022 at the beginning of the war, the sharp increase in global food prices put tens of millions of people at increased risk of acute food insecurity.

This time, the Ukrainian Agri Council, a trade group, has warned of a potential wave of bankruptcies amid the blockade, saying that “the challenges currently facing the agricultural sector are significantly more dangerous and severe in their consequences than even those of 2022.”

Wildfires this summer spared the wheat belt of France, the European Union’s largest wheat producer. But the heat has not.

France expects lower yields because of record heat this summer, according to government projections. Germany’s main farmers group said on Tuesday that yields were down for several crops, including wheat, because of drought and heat. In July, the European trade group for agricultural commodities, Coceral, issued a special bulletin, estimating lower wheat yields of 286.6 million metric tons this year, compared with 310 million metric tons in 2025, for the continent and for Britain.

Australia, also a major wheat exporter, planted fewer acres of wheat because of high fertilizer costs, stemming from the Strait of Hormuz closure.

The United States is about to have its worst wheat harvest since 1970, largely because of a terrible drought in the Great Plains, the U.S. Department of Agriculture estimated in its latest report this month. American farmers had devoted fewer acres to wheat, and yields per acre were also down.

Currently, there is enough grain stored in the silos of farmers, traders and government reserves globally.

But the smaller harvests are raising prices on the world market. Prices of U.S. soft red wheat have jumped by nearly 25 percent in the first seven months of the year, according to an analysis by Joseph Glauber, an economist with the International Food Policy Research Institute. Prices of hard red wheat have soared even more sharply. U.S. wheat stocks are down too.

“It’s not a question of availability. It’s a question of affordability,” Mr. Glauber said. “Anybody who is selling wheat will profit from the higher price.”

Rising prices of imported wheat puts enormous pressure on governments that are forced to buy high and then help subsidize the costs to keep bread prices within the reach of its people.

Egypt, which buys most of its wheat from abroad, including from Russia and Ukraine, has tried to bolster wheat production at home, with the government offering higher prices to farmers. Still, Egypt remains far from reaching anything close to self-sufficiency. There is simply not enough water to produce what the country needs.

Then there are President Trump’s tariffs. To try to avoid additional higher rates, some wheat-importing emerging economies, such as Bangladesh, agreed to buy substantial amounts of U.S. wheat.

That means they are obliged to pay whatever price U.S. wheat goes for this year, even it is substantially higher than what other countries are offering.

Analysts in Bangladesh have denounced the deal as unfair.

The perils facing the world’s breadbaskets come at a time when an El Niño, a naturally recurring weather pattern, is raising the risks of extreme weather for farmers in many parts of the world, including in countries like Ethiopia and Guatemala, where millions of small farmers subsist on what they grow on their own land.

The last El Niño event, in 2015 and 2016, worsened food insecurity for an estimated 60 million to 100 million people, the World Food Program estimated.

This time, the W.F.P. says, it could expand the ranks of those who are unable to meet their daily food needs to 274 million, up from 225 million today. The biggest effects are expected in Central America and southern Africa.

“It is naïve to think we can rely on a food system built for a different era,” Mr. Fraser said. “And so we need to reimagine how to feed ourselves.”

item.title: What Canadian Goods Will Take Trump’s 50% Tariffs? Some Pretty Strange Items.
item.description:
Anoraks and suit jackets. National flags. Some Christmas ornaments. And 36 different kinds of plywood.

The lists of hundreds of goods from Canada subject to new 50 percent tariffs from the United States is long and seemingly organized at random.

The Trump administration imposed the tariffs, which took effect on Saturday, after Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada called off trade negotiations with the United States that had lasted nearly a month. “They asked too much and offered too little,” Mr. Carney said.

Mr. Carney has promised to retaliate “dollar for dollar” against the new tariffs, which join previous tariffs of up to 50 percent that President Trump put on Canadian aluminum, steel and autos last year. Lumber has tariffs that predate Mr. Trumps’s return to office; he nevertheless increased them last year.

Here are some of the goods that are subject to the new tariffs:

For Canadian companies that depend on U.S. business, the new tariffs are likely to be a source of great anxiety. For customs brokers and trade lawyers who guide those companies, they are an extraordinary business opportunity.

But for the lay reader, the tariffs are sometimes baffling. The items affected, according to the Trump administration, cover $20 billion in Canadian exports. They are laid out in three lists, which can be found here, here and here.

Some clear patterns emerge from the text. Canada’s forest industry, which has been enmeshed in a seemingly endless battle with the United States for decades, has been particularly targeted. On the lists, the many wood products include 36 different kinds of plywood alone. Homebuilders in the United States have already said there is not enough American product to replace Canadian plywood, so the tariffs could increase housing construction costs.

Alcohol is also prominent. The Trump administration has been particularly vexed by the fact that eight of Canada’s 10 provinces still restrict U.S. wine and spirits from their government-owned liquor distribution system and stores. Those measures began after Mr. Trump suggested making Canada the 51st state and imposed tariffs in violation of the free trade agreement between the two countries and Mexico.

Some of the drinks now effectively shut out from the United States by tariffs hold little obvious appeal, including “mixtures of or with a basis of odoriferous substances with 20 to 50 percent alcohol by weight requiring only the addition of ethyl alcohol or water to be a beverage.” Left unexplained is why anyone would add more alcohol to something that is already half composed of the intoxicant.

Dairy products are another target. Canadauses production quotas and other tools to protect domestic dairy producers, who sell largely to the Canadian market, potentially limiting the effect of the new U.S. duties.

Clothing and textiles also take a hit. Like the United States, much of Canada’s clothing production moved overseas long ago, and some Canadian online retailers sell goods made abroad to U.S. customers. That, however, will not give them an out. Simply shipping things from Canada triggers the tariffs, regardless of where the products were made.

Few items of clothing escaped the tariffs. They include overcoats, anoraks, windbreakers, sleeveless jackets, cotton sweaters, T-shirts, car coats, capes, cloaks, track suits, suit jackets, blazers and dresses. Gloves, mittens and mitts are on the list unless they are related to sports.

Also included are national flags, canvas used for painting stage backdrops, tarpaulins, awnings and sun blinds.

Not every item on the list comes from large companies. Several products, including jewelry and honey, come from small, even one-person, operations.

The item descriptions range from the broad to the almost peculiarly specific. Among the latter is wood furniture “of a kind used in the bedroom and not designed for motor vehicle use.”

The tariff list has a bit of a spoilsport bent by including “articles for Christmas festivities, ornaments, not of glass or wood,” toys, including riding ones but not bikes, fishing rods, hockey sticks, skates and “festive, carnival or other entertainment articles.” Dog owners will see similar increases in the price of leashes, collars, muzzles and harnesses.

Many products — including studio television cameras and smartphones — do not appear to be manufactured in Canada at all.

Above all, the list reveals intriguing, hidden sides of Canadian industry, including companies that produce bookbinding machines, egg grading equipment, marine buoys, derricks, sand and steam blasters, stills (“not for domestic purposes”), safes and “base metal statuettes.”

And there is perhaps the finest of all exports from Canada to the United States: “wigs (partial), false beards, eyebrows and the like, of synthetic textile materials.”

item.title: Over 2,500 Killed in the Ebola Outbreak: What to Know
item.description:
More than 2,500 people have died in an Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the fastest-spreading outbreak of the virus ever recorded, according to health officials.

The outbreak, Congo’s 17th in recent decades, has tested the country’s resources. Aid cuts, including the closure last year of the U.S. Agency for International Development, have hampered the international response. Early surveillance and testing failed to identify the outbreak, and fighting in eastern Congo has displaced millions of people, making the virus even harder to trace.

The Congolese health ministry said on Saturday that the death toll had reached 2,557, as health officials struggle to curb transmission. Congo has confirmed 5,375 cases since May 17 when the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the public health agency of the African Union, announced the outbreak. Nearly half of confirmed patients are dying in this outbreak, according to the government.

“We must act at the scale the emergency demands,” said Dr. Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, said on social media on Sunday.

There are no targeted vaccines or treatments for the type of Ebola virus behind this outbreak, which is known as Bundibugyo, but clinical trials have begun in Congo for possible treatments, and for a drug that could prevent infection in people exposed to the virus.

Ituri Province in northeastern Congo, where the outbreak was first identified, remains by far the worst-affected province, health officials said.

More than 900,000 people in Ituri have been displaced by conflict, according to the United Nations, and the region’s artisanal gold mines draw laborers from a wide area. The World Health Organization has said that the high degree of population movement has made it easier for the virus to spread. It has also made contact tracing difficult.

The government says the outbreak has now spread to six provinces in eastern Congo including Haut-Uele, which borders South Sudan, and Tshopo, whose main city, Kisangani, is one of the largest in the country. Kisangani is a particular concern, health officials say, because boats ferry passengers down the Congo River from the city to the capital, Kinshasa.

In neighboring Uganda, there were 20 Ebola cases and three deaths, but health officials contained the outbreak and have recorded no new cases since June 21. Last month the country declared its outbreak over.

Congo’s health ministry said on Saturday that 737 people were currently hospitalized or in isolation. The W.H.O. has warned that many others have not been able to reach a clinic and are being cared for or dying at home.

Patients cannot always find the care they need or even food or clean drinking water. Relatives come to care for the sick or to collect bodies for burial, often without wearing protection against the highly contagious disease.

And even though Congo has been through outbreaks before, many health workers have not been trained to deal with the disease. Some have died themselves.

Health officials say they fear they are losing the battle to contain the virus.

“The epidemic is increasing faster and spreading wider than our ability to respond,” said Julien Harneis, the senior Ebola coordinator for the United Nations. “When the epidemic gets into new areas where the people working in the health system aren’t prepared, that’s where we see the heaviest toll.”

To turn the situation around, health workers say they must build more teams of professionals and volunteers trained in aspects of Ebola response, including the care of patients, the safe and dignified burial of victims, and the education of local communities about precautionary measures. Increasingly, those teams need to be deployed or activated away from the main health centers.

A particular fear is that the virus could spread to South Sudan, a country whose health system has been weakened by conflict, and to the Congolese capital, Kinshasa, one of Africa’s biggest cities.

The State Department said this month that it had committed more than $512 million to the outbreak in what it called a “rapid and comprehensive response.”

The European Commission said in July it had committed 493 million euros (around $576 million) to the effort, and other governments including Congo’s have donated smaller sums.

But public health experts and health workers say a significant obstacle to the international response is how little the United States, which once funded robust disease surveillance networks in the region, has done. The United States withdrew from the W.H.O. in January, and last year the Trump administration shut down the U.S. Agency for International Development, which played a major role in containing earlier outbreaks.

Mr. Hareneis, the U.N. Ebola coordinator, said this week that funding could run out soon.

While the outbreak is centered in Congo, citizens of other countries have contracted the virus. An American working for an evangelical disaster relief organization in Congo tested positive for Ebola, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in July. The aid worker was the second American to contract the disease, after a missionary doctor tested positive soon after the outbreak was declared on May 15.

The month before, a French doctor who had traveled to Congo tested positive for the virus.

Several countries are screening travelers or have tightened their borders.

The Trump administration has invoked a public health law, known as Title 42, to bar entry into the United States for all immigrants and U.S. permanent residents and citizens who had been in Congo, Uganda or South Sudan in the previous 21 days.

In late May, U.S. officials unveiled plans for a 50-bed quarantine center at an air base in central Kenya to house Americans who have been exposed to the virus. The project incited deadly protests in the town of Nanyuki, close to the air base, by Kenyans fearing contagion. Seven American aid workers who had recently been in Congo were quarantined at the facility in July.

During previous U.S. administrations, Americans exposed to the Ebola virus were brought home to be treated at specialized medical units.

In June, Congo’s government introduced a system to regulate travel for people who have been in affected areas, which included a 21-day quarantine in certain cases.

.

Ebola is an illness caused by a group of related viruses, known as orthoebolaviruses, which fruit bats are thought to carry without being sickened by them. Outbreaks have mostly occurred in sub-Saharan Africa. The largest began in 2014, with cases in southeastern Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, and lasted two years.

People can contract Ebola through contact with the bodily fluids of an infected, sick or dead person or with contaminated objects like clothing, bedding, needles or medical equipment.

Four of the six known species of Ebola viruses can be fatal to humans. People may first experience so-called dry symptoms such as fever, aches, pains and fatigue before progressing to wet symptoms. These include diarrhea, vomiting and bleeding, according to the C.D.C.

Vaccines and an antiviral drug have been approved for the Zaire species of Ebola, the most common one. But there is no vaccine or specific treatment for the Bundibugyo species.

Its incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, and people are usually not infectious until symptoms appear. Early symptoms like fever and fatigue resemble those of other illnesses, including malaria, so early detection can be difficult.

Fatality rates during the last two outbreaks of this form of Ebola ranged from 30 percent to 50 percent of those infected, according to the W.H.O.

Lynsey Chutel, Ephrat Livni and Amelia Nierenberg contributed reporting.
